newsitem.title: USA: Burlington falls short of on-time goals.
newsitem.headline: Burlington falls short of on-time goals.

text.p: WASHINGTON, Jan 13, Reuter - A combination of bad winter weather and problems with fusing two large rail netowrks into one caused Burlington Northern Sante Fe to fall short of its on-time performance goals in 1996, a company official said Monday.

In its first full year operating as a single railway, BNSF shipments arrived on time 87 percent of the time, slightly below its objective of 92 percent, said Paul Nowicki, BNSF assistant vice president for government and public policy.

"1996 was not a very successful year for our company in terms of service," he said, speaking to a gathering of transportation industry officials at the Transportation Research Board's annual meeting here. "We fell well short of our 92 percent on-time goal."

An unusually harsh winter in 1996 was partly to blame, he said, but the demands of combining Burlington Northern Inc with Sante Fe Pacific Corp to create the second-largest railroad in the U.S. also took an unanticipated toll.
"We were still pretty much at arms' length the entire year," he said of the two systems. "We were changing (rail)cars back and forth, and not using the more efficient, more direct routes."

BNSF shipments of carload merchandise, which includes chemicals, forest products and consumer items, fared worst during the year, while coal freight scored the best overall on-time performance, he said.

The company expects most of the glitches will be ironed out by mid-1997, when computer systems from the two rail networks are fused into one. While BNSF has yet to set its on-time performance goals for 1997, Nowicki said the company will likely set its sights on 92 percent again this year.
Despite the difficulties BNSF has experienced during the transition to one railroad, Nowicki hailed the recent spate of rail link-ups in the U.S. as key to the industry's continued vibrancy.
"Mergers have been a very critical ingredient in the renaissance of American railroads," he said. "There have been far more benefits than pitfalls from these mergers."
BNSF expects to reap an additional $306 million in revenues annually as a result of service improvements made possible by the merger.

Of that growth, about 60 percent came from market share previously controlled by other railroads, Nowicki said, though he conceded that BNSF's newly-merged western rival, Union Pacific Southern Pacific Corp, could cut into the projected revenue upturn.
"Their merger is going to have some impact," Nowicki said. (Union Pacific) is in a better position to protect their revenue (share)."
